newsitem.title: JAPAN: North Korea says U.S. pledged to provide food aid.
newsitem.headline: North Korea says U.S. pledged to provide food aid.

text.p: The United States has pledged to ease a trade embargo against North Korea and give food aid to the flood-ravaged communist state, Pyongyang's official news agency said on Monday.
Washington struck the deals during talks in New York between officials from the United States and North Korea from December 9 to 29, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said.

"The U.S. side promised that it would take additional measures to ease the embargo on the DPRK (North Korea) and supply food to the DPRK," KCNA said in a dispatch monitored in Tokyo. It gave no details.
On Sunday, North Korea apologised for the first time for an incursion by one of its submarines into South Korean waters in September, expressing "deep regret" in a brief statement.

The statement was issued after intense bargaining in New York between U.S. and North Korean officials on a choice of words to make the apology acceptable to Seoul, which branded the incursion a "military provocation".
U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Sunday he welcomed North Korea's apology for the submarine's incursion.
Clinton called North Korea's apology a "significant development, which I hope will contribute to the reduction of tensions on the Korean peninsula."
The reclusive North Korea has been suffering from famine after two consecutive years of serious flooding.

Officials and diplomats close to the talks said on Sunday the U.N. World Food Programme plans to issue another appeal in the next few weeks, at which time Washington may pledge about $6 million worth of food aid.
In addition, Washington could issue a license to allow grain company Cargill to export a reported 500,000 tonnes of food in a barter transaction it is seeking, they said.
The submarine incident had scuttled a process of engagement intended to bring North Korea out of its isolation, revamp its nuclear programme and help ease its famine.
South Korea has informally blocked further food aid to the North since the submarine incursion.
In Monday's dispatch, North Korea's mouthpiece KCNA said Pyongyang voiced its willingness to take part in a joint briefing by Washington and Seoul on proposed four-nation peace talks.
"The DPRK side expressed its willingness to allow the resumption of spent fuel storage and listen to a 'joint explanation' of the proposed 'four-way talks'," KCNA said.

Both Koreas originally were reluctant to participate, but North Korea recently had begun moving toward accepting a "briefing" on the proposals from the United States and South Korea. The North wanted pre-conditions, such as lifting of trade sanctions and help on food aid,

Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam proposed in April that they join with China and North Korea in peace talks aimed at securing a peace agreement to replace the truce accord that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
"At the talks, the sides reaffirmed their commitment to implement the agreed framework and continue to promote bilateral relations," KCNA said.
